title: Set four drift-fence arms tight against a pitfall trap
instruction: Set up the drift fence around the black pitfall trap: for each of the four orange pegs, stand one wooden board on its long narrow edge along the line from the trap's centre to that peg, with the board's inner end right up against the trap's rim but not over its opening. Then let go of every board and lift the grippers clear.
context: Ecological consultants and wildlife biologists survey ground-dwelling reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates with pitfall traps (buckets sunk flush with the ground) fed by drift fences: low barriers that animals follow until they drop in. In Y and cross arrays several arms radiate from one hub trap. Each arm is staked out, then set straight along its line with its end butted to the hub's rim. A gap lets animals walk round the trap; on a hub fed by four arms, an arm end over the mouth blocks the other arms' entry, so this protocol treats any overlap as a failed set-up. Methods: Corn 1994, 'Straight-line drift fences and pitfall traps', in Heyer et al. (eds.), Measuring and Monitoring Biological Diversity: Standard Methods for Amphibians; USGS Techniques and Methods 2-A5. Workers: Zoologists and Wildlife Biologists (O*NET 19-1023.00), Biological Technicians (19-4021.00), Environmental Science and Protection Technicians (19-4042.00).
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. Bearings are measured anticlockwise from +x, seen from above, about the trap's centre. Three kinds of thing are on the table. (1) Pitfall trap: a black-painted plywood (or rubber) disc, 70 mm across and 3 mm tall, fixed to the table, centred at x 27.0 cm, y 0. It stands for the open mouth of a bucket sunk flush with the ground; its rim is its 35 mm radius. (2) Four pegs: orange-painted wooden dowels, 12 mm across and 60 mm tall, fixed upright on the table with their centres 200 mm from the trap's centre at bearings 45, 135, 225 and 315 degrees: peg 1 at x 41.14 cm, y +14.14 cm; peg 2 at x 12.86 cm, y +14.14 cm; peg 3 at x 12.86 cm, y -14.14 cm; peg 4 at x 41.14 cm, y -14.14 cm. Each marks the far end of one fence arm. Line k runs from the trap's centre to peg k's centre; lines 1 and 3, and lines 2 and 4, continue each other through the trap. (3) Four fence boards: loose planed pine blocks, unpainted, 130 x 20 x 50 mm (length x thickness x height), 65 g each, all alike (any board may go on any line). Each stands on one of its 130 x 20 mm edges with its long side along x, centred at x 24.0 cm and y +37.0 cm, +45.0 cm, -37.0 cm and -45.0 cm: two beside each arm's base, 60 mm apart face to face. The boards are placed so that each arm sets its own side's two fence arms: the boards at y +37.0 and +45.0 cm are within gripping reach of the left arm only, those at y -37.0 and -45.0 cm of the right arm only. Nothing marks the lines on the table, and nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The scorer reads the four boards' poses every control step and, from the embodiment's state, each gripper's tool point (TCP). 'Footprint': a board's outline seen from above (the outline of all its corners), standing or not. 'Gap': the distance in plan from the trap's centre to the nearest point of a board's footprint, minus 35 mm (negative when the outline is inside the rim). 'Standing': the board's 50 mm axis within 10 degrees of vertical, its lowest point within 3 mm of the table top, and at rest: every position of its centre over the last 0.5 s within 2 mm of the current one (positions only; speeds are not used). 'Free': no gripper TCP that is less than 90 mm above the table is within 60 mm, in plan, of the board's footprint (fully open, a finger pad reaches 56 mm from its TCP, so a pad touching a board makes it not free). 'Sector': each board belongs to the peg whose bearing from the trap's centre is nearest the bearing of the board's centre (four 90 degree sectors centred on 45, 135, 225 and 315 degrees). Line k is fenced when a board in sector k is standing and free, its long axis is within 8 degrees of the direction from the trap's centre to peg k (either end may face the trap), the trap's centre is within 10 mm, in plan, of the board's long centre line, and its gap is from -1 mm to +10 mm. A board can fence only its own sector's line, and each line counts once. Score 0 if at the scored step any board, standing, lying, held or not, has a gap below -1 mm (its outline more than 1 mm inside the rim: on or over the opening; the 1 mm allows for contact against the disc's edge). Otherwise 0.25 for each line fenced: 1.0 all four lines; 0.75 three; 0.5 two; 0.25 one; 0 none (for example the boards at their starts, boards laid round the trap tangentially, or all four on their lines with 15 mm gaps). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Success (all four lines fenced, nothing over the rim) held for 1 s ends the trial; otherwise the score is read at the last step. Examples: one arm's two boards on lines 1 and 2: 0.5; two boards on lines 3 and 4 only: 0.5 (they do not also fence lines 1 and 2, which continue them); three good boards and the fourth turned 12 degrees: 0.75; four good boards, one still gripped (TCP 35 mm up): 0.75 until it is let go and the gripper's TCP rises to 90 mm above the table or is more than 60 mm, in plan, from the board's outline; four good boards, one end 3 mm over the rim: 0; a board lying flat on its line: that line is not fenced; a board across the trap: 0; two boards in one sector: that line counts once. On a step where the arms cannot be read, every board counts as free. On a real rig everything is judged after the arms withdraw: the gap with a feeler gauge or a 10 mm gauge block between board and rim, the angle and the centre-line offset from a top photo or by sighting along a string from the trap's centre to the peg's centre, standing with a small square or a phone level.
fidelity: A tabletop model of a cross-shaped pitfall and drift-fence array with arms shortened to 130 mm (real arms run 5 to 15 m). Real fences are flexible sheet or mesh buried 10 to 20 cm deep; here they are rigid pine boards standing on the surface. The trap is a fixed 3 mm black disc standing in for a flush bucket mouth. Rigid bodies, one friction for everything. 'Let go' is judged from the gripper TCPs (60 mm in plan, beyond an open finger pad's reach), not from finger contact.
reset_notes: Stand the four boards back on their 130 x 20 mm edges at their starts (x 24.0 cm; y +37.0, +45.0, -37.0 and -45.0 cm), long sides along x. The trap and the pegs are fixed. Nothing is consumed.
